claims.claim: The fornication is unsentimental but has a certain imaginative élan (the purple-bearded drunk lapping wine off a wench's breasts).
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: unsentimental fornication that is not without a certain imaginative élan

claims.claim: Brutal, irreversible consequences for characters' actions are part of the epic's distinctive tone and feel more 'literary' than any television series.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue

claims.claim: Abandoning the core characters for new ones in the fourth book was a serious misstep; the reviewer took a month because he did not care about the strangers.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: I simply didn’t care about these strangers

claims.claim: Cersei's sword-versus-moonblood speech is an arresting echo of the Greek notion that childbirth is for women what war is for men; Martin carries argument in character monologue.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: an arresting echo of the Greek notion

claims.claim: The theological preoccupations do not raise the books to Lord of the Rings' level of parable; the appeal is thematic ambition plus richly satisfying details.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue

claims.claim: Each chapter is narrated in the third person from one character's point of view; eight major viewpoint characters in book one grew to seventeen by A Feast for Crows.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: Each chapter is narrated in the third person

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a 'gardener' who has a rough destination but improvises, in contrast to Tolkien the 'architect' who built languages and histories first.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: he has a rough idea where he’s going but improvises

claims.claim: Martin fleshes out only as much world as the story needs and has invented only seven words of High Valyrian.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: I’ve invented seven words of High Valyrian

claims.claim: Martin drew on the Wars of the Roses rather than mythology, used relatively little magic, and the result felt dangerous, lusty and real.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: it felt dangerous, lusty, and real

claims.claim: Martin suspects he rewrites too much, ripping one Tyrion chapter out and putting it back for ten years, even trying it as a dream sequence.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011

claims.claim: Aligning the chronologies of seventeen viewpoint characters' travel times across two books bedevils the writing.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: The ‘Dance’ timeline alone is a bitch and a half

claims.claim: Fans catch small continuity slips (a horse that changes sex, eyes green then blue) because every line is analysed.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: People are analyzing every goddam line in these books

claims.claim: The narrative is intricate and racy, practically custom-built for HBO ('The Sopranos in Middle-earth').
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011

claims.claim: Martin's taste for pageantry and colour (his medieval miniature dioramas) carries into the fiction.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: I like the pageantry and the color

claims.claim: More than a thousand named characters exist by a superfan's count; Martin quotes Tolkien that the tale grew in the telling.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: The tale grew in the telling

verdicts.trueWording: unsentimental fornication that is not without a certain imaginative elan
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the purple-bearded drunk pouring wine over a wench's breasts 'so he might lap it off' is the article's own next sentence. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: brutal, irreversible real-life consequences ... part of the distinctive tone
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: such consequences are 'part of the distinctive tone of Martin's epic', and the willingness to mete out harsh consequences 'feels more authentic, more "literary" than anything even the best series in this new golden age of television can provide.' Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: one of the few serious missteps ... I simply didn't care about these strangers
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: abandoning most characters and locales in the fourth novel was 'one of the few serious missteps'; 'it took me a month to get through the fourth, because I simply didn't care about these strangers.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: an arresting echo of the Greek notion ... childbirth ... what warfare is for men
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The Cersei speech on the page runs sword/lance/mace against 'birth and moonblood'; the article introduces it as making Cersei's thwarted independence 'clear in a remarkable speech she is given', so the argument-in-monologue limb is supported. Page says 'warfare', claim says 'war'.

verdicts.trueWording: theological preoccupations do not raise them to the level of Lord of the Rings
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: the theological preoccupations do not raise the novels 'to the level of, say, Lord of the Rings', whose clash gives it 'the high Aeschylean sheen of political parable'; appeal lies 'as much in its thematic ambitions as in its richly satisfying details.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: narrated in the third person, from the point of view of a single character
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: 'The first book had eight major viewpoint characters, but by "A Feast for Crows" the total for the series had grown to seventeen.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: he thinks of himself as a gardener; Tolkien was what Martin calls an architect
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: gardener 'has a rough idea where he's going but improvises along the way'; 'Tolkien created entire languages, mythologies, and histories for Middle-earth long before he wrote the novels set there.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: fleshes out only as much of his imaginary world as he needs
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim inside Martin's reply to fans asking for a High Valyrian grammar. Page qualifies with 'sometimes fleshes out only as much...as he needs to make a workable setting for the story'; claim's compression does not change the sense.

verdicts.trueWording: from history instead of from mythology ... relatively little magic
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: 'he based his tale, loosely, on the Wars of the Roses'; 'Martin's story contained relatively little magic, and it felt dangerous, lusty, and real.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: tinkering with some parts of A Dance with Dragons for ten years
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim ('Maybe I'm rewriting too much,' he suggested; 'Maybe I have perfectionist's disease'). Page: ten years of tinkering is the topic sentence, illustrated immediately by the Tyrion chapter - 'I ripped it out and put it back in... Then I put it in as a dream sequence, and then I ripped it out again.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: making sure that the chronologies of the different stories line up has particularly bedevilled Martin
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim from Martin's blog post as reproduced. Page: seventeen viewpoint characters by A Feast for Crows; 'How long is it going to take this character to get from point A to point B by ship? Meanwhile, what's happened in the other book?' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a horse that changes sex between books; eyes green in one passage, blue in another
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and Martin adds 'if I make a mistake they're going to nail me on it.' Page: 'My fans point them out to me.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the book's intricate, racy narrative practically feels custom-built for HBO
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page attributes 'The Sopranos in Middle-earth' to David Benioff, who 'now winces at the formulation'; Miller says 'it remains sound'. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I like the pageantry and the color - said of his medieval miniatures
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and the dioramas of mostly medieval miniatures are on the page. But the page never says this taste carries into the fiction: the only bridge it draws from the closets to the novels is population - 'Like his closets, Martin's head is crammed with people' - leading to Garcia's thousand-name census, not to pageantry or colour in the prose.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the pageantry-and-colour taste carries into the fiction

verdicts.trueWording: by Garcia's count, more than a thousand named characters
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: "'The tale grew in the telling,' Martin often says, quoting J. R. R. Tolkien." Page separately calls Garcia 'a superfan'. All limbs supported, though the two facts sit in different sections of the piece.
